person: New mother in Ghana, extended family household
situation: A new mother in Ghana faces pressure from her grandmother (primary caregiver figure) to apply traditional cord-care substances — shea butter, toothpaste, or a leaf-and-salt mixture — to the baby's umbilical cord stump.
trigger: Grandmother observes the cord and offers to apply her preferred substance; the mother is caught between clinical guidance (from a clinic/health worker) and deeply rooted traditional practice.
context: 63% of unapproved cord dressings in Ghana are applied by grandmothers (PMC6630491). The grandmother's authority in the household is absolute on child-care matters. The mother may not have direct access to a clinic or health worker at the moment of decision.
behaviour: Mother accepts grandmother's intervention (most common outcome per the research)
Mother may attempt to resist but lacks the language or authority to override
Mother may seek validation from health worker (if accessible) to counter grandmother

failed_attempts.tried: Mother may have tried to follow clinic advice but grandmother overruled

constraint: Grandmother is the primary caregiver figure; the mother's authority is subordinate in the household hierarchy; traditional practices are deeply rooted and carry social weight.
thought: My grandmother raised all of us with shea butter and we turned out fine. The clinic may be right but grandmother knows best.
fear: Defying grandmother's authority; being seen as an ungrateful or ignorant daughter; the cord falling off 'too slowly' if traditional methods aren't applied.
emotional_stake: Torn between two authority systems (clinic vs grandmother) with no clear resolution path.
exact_language: Shea butter is applied to the cord stump because it is believed to hasten cord separation. Some grandmothers use toothpaste or a leaf-and-salt mixture.
desired_change: A culturally respectful way to explain why the cord needs to dry naturally, without offending the grandmother or undermining her authority.

evidence_source.excerpt: 63% of unapproved cord dressings are applied by grandmothers...Shea butter is applied to the cord stump because it is believed to hasten cord separation.
evidence_source.context: Qualitative focus group study in Ghana (Asante-Darko & Norvishis, 2019). 54.8% of caregivers believe the cord falls off by day 4, contributing to anxiety when it doesn't.

relationships: Same grandmother-authority pattern as CRF-PPL-CORD-CARE-005 (Nigerian household, binder); Ghana variant adds shea butter/toothpaste/leaf-salt substances
Same generational-advice conflict as CRF-PPL-CORD-CARE-004 (American context, alcohol); Ghana variant is substance-specific
